proposals.before: The crown prince's golden carriage was to follow the upper duke's standard of nine as the measure, reduced by one quarter.
proposals.after: For the named items and colors of the emperor's golden carriage, following the upper duke's standard of nine as the measure, one quarter was to be reduced.
proposals.reason: Chinese 上用金輅 refers to the emperor's golden carriage as the model being reduced; the idiomatic English wrongly makes the crown prince's carriage the grammatical subject.

proposals.before: Where the sovereign himself trod the ground his carriage reached—unlike mere display pieces—the foot-rest, back-rest, and footway cushions were all of red brocade, while seat cushions, traveling-horse cushions, and three sheer hanging curtains used silver-brown, yellow, and green brocade.
proposals.after: Where the sovereign himself trod the ground his carriage reached—unlike mere display pieces—the foot-rest, back-rest, and footway cushions were all of red brocade, while seat cushions, railing-barrier cushions, and three sheer hanging curtains used silver-brown, yellow, and green brocade.
proposals.reason: 行馬褥 denotes cushions for the 行馬 (railing barriers/trestles), not 'traveling-horse cushions'.

proposals.before: Grand Preceptor, three dukes, princes, and first-rank chief ministers wore large single-stem floral brocade no more than five cun across; chief councillors wore small single-stem floral brocade no more than three cun.
proposals.after: The Three Preceptors, three dukes, princes, and first-rank chief ministers wore large single-stem floral brocade no more than five cun across; chief councillors wore small single-stem floral brocade no more than three cun.
proposals.reason: Chinese 三師 means the Three Preceptors (Grand Preceptor, Grand Tutor, Grand Guardian), not Grand Preceptor alone; literal already expands them.

proposals.before: Fifth rank and above wore court dress when hurrying to audience and spread-black boots at the ministry; rain or snow permitted convenience.
proposals.after: Fifth rank and above wore court dress when hurrying to audience and spread black (zhan zao) dress at the ministry; rain or snow permitted convenience.
proposals.reason: 展皁 parallels 展紫 as a dress color mode, not boots; the Chinese has no footwear term.

proposals.before: Officials fifth rank and above: hurrying to court then court dress, going to the ministry then spread-black boots; if rain or snow stained clothing they followed convenience.
proposals.after: Officials fifth rank and above: hurrying to court then court dress, going to the ministry then spread black; if rain or snow stained clothing they followed convenience.
proposals.reason: 展皁 is dress mode like 展紫, not boots.

proposals.before: Hanlin officials, Veritable Record compilers, remonstrance officers, secretaries, and clerks wore rank dress and colored belts at court, narrow purple and gold belt on duty.
proposals.after: Hanlin Academy officials, compilers of the Veritable Record, remonstrance officials, secretaries, and secretarial clerks: when attending court and standing in attendance they wore their rank's dress and colored belt.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic invents 'narrow purple and gold belt on duty' from the next unit s0252; Chinese s0251 ends at 色帶.

proposals.after: Beside the bands hung pearl-knotted cords half the belt's length—the type Prince Hailing bestowed on Daxingguo.
proposals.reason: 大興國 is the personal name of Hailing's attendant Daxingguo, not a place called Daxing.

proposals.after: Beside the bands pearl knotted cords half the belt length hung down—the kind Prince Hailing bestowed on Daxingguo.

decisions.reason: s0080's topic is 上用金輅名件色數 (named items and colors of the emperor's golden carriage), reduced by one quarter from the upper-duke standard of nine; the idiomatic wrongly makes the crown prince's carriage the grammatical subject.
In s0015, 行馬褥 are cushions for 行馬 (railing barriers/trestles used with carriages), not traveling-horse cushions; the proposed replacement restores the correct sense.
Same error as the idiomatic field: s0015 行馬褥 denotes cushions for railing barriers/trestles, not traveling horses.
s0050 lists 畫梯、托叉、行馬 as carriage fittings; 行馬 here are railing barriers/trestles, not traveling horses.
Literal s0050 likewise mistranslates 行馬 as traveling horses; railing barriers is the correct ritual sense.
s0054's 金塗銅葉段行馬二 are gilt-bronze leaf-segment railing barriers among carriage fittings, not traveling horses.
Literal s0054 has the same 行馬 mistranslation; replacing traveling horses with railing barriers matches the Chinese inventory item.
s0225 begins 三師、三公; 三師 are the Three Preceptors as a class, not the Grand Preceptor alone. The proposed 'Three Preceptors' matches the Chinese.

decisions.after: Fifth rank and above wore court dress when hurrying to audience and spread black at the ministry; rain or snow permitted convenience.
decisions.reason: s0246 赴省則展皁 parallels s0247 展紫 as a dress mode, with no footwear term; 'spread-black boots' is wrong. The proposal correctly removes boots, but the parenthetical '(zhan zao) dress' is awkward; 'spread black' matches the chapter's own rendering of 展紫.
Literal likewise invents boots for 展皁; 'spread black' correctly treats it as the dress mode parallel to 展紫.
s0251 ends at 色帶; 'narrow purple and gold belt on duty' belongs only to the next unit s0252 (當直則窄紫、金帶) and must not be merged into this sentence.

decisions.reason: s0279 海陵賜大興國 names the person 大興國 (Daxingguo), not a place 'Daxing'; the proposed personal-name rendering is correct.
Literal 'Daxing State' wrongly splits 大興國 as a polity; it is Hailing's attendant's personal name, so Daxingguo is required.
